articles.title: Could tomato paste help your brain? A three-month trial points to modest gains in attention and memory
articles.summary: Tomatoes are the main dietary source of lycopene, a red pigment that can reach the brain. In a new trial, daily tomato paste was linked to better attention and memory scores, along with preliminary changes in how certain brain networks communicate.

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? articles.title: Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch
articles.summary: A common, inexpensive medication could hold an unexpected clue to preventing dementia. Researchers found that older adults with a specific genetic profile had a 70% lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin, even though previous studies found no overall protective effect. The discovery suggests that genetics could help explain why some people benefit while others do not.

articles.title: This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans
articles.summary: For nearly a century, people in distant parts of the world have reported a bizarre experience after eating certain wild mushrooms: seeing dozens or even hundreds of tiny, colorful humans moving through the real world. Now, scientists have identified a mushroom species, Lanmaoa asiatica, responsible for these extraordinary hallucinations in China and the Philippines.

articles.summary: A disorganized home is often linked to poor academic performance, but a large twin study reveals that shared genetics and broader family environments are to blame, not the noise and clutter itself.

articles.title: Autistic children’s brains respond less to the emotional meaning of sentences, fMRI study finds
articles.summary: When children hear a sentence about someone’s feelings, part of the brain’s language system typically responds more strongly than it does to a sentence about objects. In autistic children, that difference was smaller.

articles.title: PaperFormalizer: Author-in-the-Loop Autoformalization of Research Papers in Lean
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.31810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Even a carefully proofread paper can leave small gaps in its proofs or its stated assumptions. We introduce PaperFormalizer, a Lean-based agentic pipeline that helps authors find and close such gaps in their own papers and turn each paper into a Lean-verified version. Starting from the LaTeX source, PaperFormalizer transcribes the paper into a dependency graph of statements, audits each statement in natural language for faithfulness, ambiguity and correctness, and then formalizes and proves the statements in Lean against Mathlib, optional domain

articles.title: Collaborative In-Context Learning for Indoor Radio Map Estimation
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.31702v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Indoor radio map estimation (RME) is essential for wireless applications such as coverage planning, localization, and network deployment. However, most existing methods follow a supervised learning paradigm that requires costly labeled data and task-specific model training. Moreover, indoor environments involve privacy-sensitive information, such as building layouts and structures, that often cannot be centralized. To address these challenges, we make the first attempt to formulate indoor RME as a collaborative in-context learning (ICL) problem.

articles.title: Does LeWorldModel Preserve Local Action Geometry?
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.31716v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine how closely pretrained LeWorldModel (LeWM) reproduces the effects of small action changes. Using matched simulator and model responses, we measure action sensitivity with Gram matrices at three perturbation scales. Across nearly a thousand states from Reacher and OGBench Cube, the most sensitive action directions differ by median angles of about $36^\circ$ and $42^\circ$, respectively, at the smallest scale. Increasing the perturbation tenfold reduces median normalized Gram discrepancy by roughly 70\% on Reacher and 47\% on Cube. Geome

articles.title: News coverage of psilocybin often outpaces the science, systematic review finds
articles.summary: Researchers compared 70 psilocybin trial publications with 172 news articles. Both reported positive results at similar rates, but news coverage tended to present the benefits as established and rarely discussed the small, early-stage nature of the research.

articles.title: Just a few minutes of speech may offer a window into brain health and aging
articles.summary: Researchers trained a machine learning model to estimate a person’s age from short voice recordings. In a study of nearly 3,000 adults across Latin America, speech in people with dementia tended to sound older than in cognitively healthy adults.

articles.title: Glutamate receptors may help explain the brain structure behind children’s math and reading abilities
articles.summary: Of 19 chemical signaling systems examined, only one consistently matched the brain structure linked to children’s math and reading abilities across two independent groups: NMDA receptors, which respond to the neurotransmitter glutamate.

articles.title: We’ll pay to get revenge on an algorithm, even though it can’t feel a thing
articles.summary: An algorithm can’t feel the sting of losing money, but people will sacrifice their own cash to punish one anyway. In experiments with more than 6,000 participants, people retaliated against unfair machines just as often as against unfair humans.
